orders.rationale: Both answers are accurate. B is more complete: it adds when signing began, when the Constitution was ratified, and when the government started operating in 1789. It also cites specific sources inline. A leaves out ratification and 1789, and its listed sources are vague and not tied to its claims. B ends with a clear one-line summary.

Both answers are accurate. A gives July 4, 1776, clarifies that signing began August 2, and adds the 1783 treaty, the 1787 Constitution, its 1788 ratification and the 1789 start of the federal government. That clearly separates the nation's founding from its current government. B is correct and mentions the July 2 Lee Resolution, but stops at 1787 and never says when the current government began.

Both answers are correct and complete. A gives the exact election date. B says Obama held office "for all of 2016" and backs every claim with one fitting source. A's citations point to the election and Trump articles, not to an Obama source. Neither has errors that matter, so this is a tie.

Both correctly name Barack Obama, give accurate term dates, and explain that Trump won in November 2016 but took office in January 2017. A states clearly that Obama served all of 2016, and its source covers its claims. B adds the correct election date, but cites election and Trump pages for Obama's term. Neither is clearly better.

B explains that the length depends on the end point, with correct figures: Western ~500 years (476), Eastern ~1,480 years (1453), Roman state ~2,200 years from 753 BC. A gets the core 1,480-year figure right but adds an irrelevant, doubtful area figure and lists an unused source.

A is better: its dates and spans are right (about 500 years for the West, about 1,480 to 1453, about 2,200 from 753 BC), and it explains why the answer depends on the end date. B gets the 1,480-year figure right but pads with off-topic facts, including an area of 5,957,000 km² that I couldn't verify, and it lists source [3] without citing it.

B is accurate and complete. It covers Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis (including his 1931 firing and 2007 recognition), Morrow and Paine, all with fitting sources. A is garbled: it repeats Morrow, uses the odd phrase "masterwork architect," mentions Ellis without saying what he did, leaves out Moisseiff, and gives Morrow credit for the "bridge within a bridge" without clear support.

A is accurate and complete. It names Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis, Morrow and Paine, and gets Ellis's 1931 firing and 2007 recognition right. B is garbled. It calls Strauss the "masterwork architect" when he was the chief engineer. It plays down Ellis's central role, leaves out Moisseiff, and reads awkwardly.

A wrongly says Heinlein's 1947 novel was the first fictional rocket ship, though rocket ships appeared in 1920s–30s pulps and Frau im Mond. Its source doesn't support "first." B gives accurate facts on Goddard, the V-2 and Vostok/Korolev. It also explains the ambiguity well, with sources that back each claim.

A is accurate on every point: Goddard in 1926, the V-2 reaching space in 1944, and Vostok 1 with Korolev as chief designer. It also covers the different meanings of "rocket ship." B wrongly says Rocket Ship Galileo (1947) was the first fictional rocket ship, when many earlier ones exist. B also builds its conclusion on that error and gives no detail on Goddard.

A treats outcomes as goals. The revolution did end the monarchy and create a republic, but its first plan was a constitutional monarchy. A also turns its source's description of ideas spreading into a stated aim. B correctly says the goals changed over time and covers the attack on the Ancien Régime, Enlightenment ideals and the motto. Its sources support these points.

A is better. It accurately explains that the aims changed, from constitutional monarchy to republic, and covers the key ideals and events. B treats outcomes (overthrowing the monarchy, founding a republic) as the original goal, which is wrong because early revolutionaries wanted a constitutional monarchy. B also misreads its source by saying the Revolution "aimed" to spread its ideas, and it is thin.

B answers "who really" directly: no single creator, Gilbert as the usual answer, then an accurate line from Thales to Maxwell, plus the Edison/Tesla misconception. A has correct facts but never answers directly. Its "Meanwhile" wrongly places Franklin alongside Faraday. It omits Volta and Maxwell, and some claims lack citations.

A is accurate, explains why no one person "created" electricity, and covers the key figures (Gilbert, Gray, Franklin, Volta, Faraday, Maxwell) with a clear verdict. B is mostly accurate but thinner: it omits Volta and Maxwell, gives no conclusion, and cites no source for its Gilbert and Browne claims.

B is better. It explains Rayleigh scattering, why the sky isn't violet, and how our eyes' color receptors make mixed skylight look blue rather than green. Its sources are credible. A's reasoning on green is vague, its aurora claim is doubtful, it never covers how the eye perceives the color, and it relies on weak sources, some listed but never cited.

A explains why Rayleigh scattering's 1/λ⁴ rise favors blue rather than green, covers violet, and explains color perception. Its claim that ozone absorbs violet is shaky. B is vague and doesn't really explain "not green". Its claim about green skies near auroras is muddled, and its sources are weak (a student journal and english.stackexchange).

A is accurate but thin: it never explains how the coil keeps turning and lists a car-engine source it doesn't use. B is also accurate and explains the Lorentz force, how the commutator reverses the current, and brushless and induction motors. It also notes the combustion-engine meaning. B is far more complete and useful.

Answer A explains the Lorentz force, how the commutator keeps the coil turning, and brushless and induction motors, and it notes how combustion engines differ. Its claims are accurate and backed by its sources. Answer B is also correct but only names the principle without explaining how torque is sustained, so it says little about how a motor actually works.

A is accurate but vague: it never explains slicing or the main printing methods, and it adds an odd aside about space use. B correctly covers the whole process (CAD model, STL file, slicer, layers) and explains FDM, SLA and SLS accurately, with sources that fit. B is clearer and more useful.

A gives an accurate walkthrough: CAD model, STL file, slicing, then building layer by layer. It also explains FDM, SLA and SLS correctly, including why SLS needs no supports. B is vague and generic. It applies 'material cools' to every method, though that only fits filament printing, and it adds an off-topic microgravity aside. B never explains slicing or the different printing technologies.

A doesn't explain how planes go fast. It only compares the priorities of business jets and airlines, and lists three sources it never cites. B answers directly: jet thrust, lift carrying the weight, thin air at cruise altitude, and a streamlined shape. Its figures are accurate (Mach 0.85 ≈ 900 km/h), and it explains that drag rises sharply near the speed of sound.

A answers the question directly and accurately. It covers jet thrust, wings providing lift so engines only fight drag, thin air at high altitude, and why airliners stay just below the speed of sound. Its cruise figures are correct. B never explains how planes go fast. It only compares the speed priorities of business jets and airlines, and lists sources it never uses.

B is better. It names the real sources of concern (IARC's 2B label, the NTP rat study, the 2026 HHS/FDA moves) and weighs each against the stronger evidence, including the 2024 WHO review and blinded EHS tests. A is vague and leans on Q&A forums. It also suggests, without support, that higher-power WiFi could harm health.

A is better. It explains where the worry comes from (the IARC 2B label, the NTP rat study, 2026 HHS/FDA moves), weighs the stronger evidence (the WHO 2024 review, non-ionizing physics, EHS blind trials) and notes open questions, all with relevant sources. B is vague and leans on Stack Exchange posts. Its claim that a stronger WiFi device could harm health is misleading.

B is better. It correctly says no one invented government, which grew out of Neolithic surpluses and early states such as Sumer. It also covers early theory from Plato, Aristotle and Hobbes, and those claims are accurate. A looks only at 17th–18th-century thinkers and leaves out ancient origins. Its claim that mixed government came "later" gets the order wrong, since the idea dates back to antiquity.

A is accurate: government developed gradually after the Neolithic Revolution, starting in Sumer and other early civilizations, and A also names early theorists (Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes) with support from its sources. B is vague and misleading. It points to Enlightenment thinkers as if the idea began in the 17th–18th centuries, and wrongly says mixed government came later, though it dates to antiquity.

A is accurate but thin. It lists heating methods without explaining how heat is made, how temperature is controlled, or how food cooks. B correctly covers electric resistance elements, gas burners, the thermostat cycling on and off, the three ways heat reaches food, convection fans and microwaves. Its sources support each claim, and it reads clearly on a phone.

A is accurate and covers electric and gas heating, thermostat cycling, the ways heat reaches food, convection fans and microwaves. Its one slip: infrared from the elements heats the walls and food far more than the air. B is too vague to explain how an oven actually works and lists heating methods with no detail. A is clearly better.

B is accurate and more complete: families, snout, teeth, salt glands, range, species count and color, with sources. A repeats the snout point and oversimplifies the teeth: alligators do show upper teeth when closed. Its aggression statistic is loosely supported and adds little.

A is accurate and covers snout, teeth, salt glands, range, coexistence in Florida and color. B repeats the snout point. It also wrongly says all of an alligator's teeth are hidden when its mouth is closed; the upper teeth stay visible. B's statistic about dangerous species doesn't really separate crocodiles from alligators.

B is accurate and complete: it covers coat, the cheetah's tear lines, body build and range, and it mentions black panthers. A has the basic rosette differences right but misses the tear lines and range. Its uncited 'four big cats in Acinonyx' claim is muddled and off-topic. B is clearer and more useful.

A is better: it accurately separates the cats by coat, face (tear lines), build and range. Its body-shape details are uncited but true. B gets rosettes right but omits tear lines and location. It adds a muddled, irrelevant claim about "four big cats" and the genus Acinonyx, and cites few of its listed sources.

B is accurate and more complete. It covers founders, rejection of the Vedas, atman vs. anatta, Brahman/God, dependent arising and caste, and it notes that Hinduism is diverse. A is mostly correct but thin. It mentions anatman without contrasting it with the Hindu atman, and it omits scripture and caste. A's claim about shared deities is also loosely stated.

A is accurate and covers the main differences: founder, Vedic authority, atman versus anatta, Brahman or God versus dependent arising, and caste. It also notes that Hinduism is internally diverse. B is thinner. It skips atman, Vedic authority and caste, and its summary only repeats earlier points. Its claim that both share deities such as Ganesha is loosely stated.

A gets the key fact wrong: it says baking soda makes CO2 when it gets wet, but it needs an acid. It also suggests all baking powder is double-acting. B correctly puts the difference down to acid and explains double-acting powder, why some recipes use both, and why you can't swap them one-to-one. B is accurate and practical.

A gets the chemistry right: soda needs an acid, and powder contains its own acid plus a starch. It also explains double-acting powder and when to use both. B wrongly says soda reacts with water alone and implies all baking powder is double-acting. B's swap ratio is fine, but its formula is written in LaTeX code that may not display on a phone.

B is accurate: Mongol Empire about 24M km², Rome about 5M km² under Trajan, Hadrian's withdrawal, and a correct 4–5x ratio. A falsely says Rome was "limited to Europe," gives no areas, credits a "computed" ratio to a forum post, and uses questionable population figures. B is clearly better.

Both say correctly that the Mongol Empire was larger. A gives accurate figures: about 24M vs about 5M km², Trajan's peak, Hadrian's withdrawal and the British Empire comparison. B wrongly says Rome's territory was "limited to Europe," but Rome also covered North Africa and the Middle East. B also gives no area figures and leans on a StackExchange source.

Both are accurate: espresso has more caffeine per ounce, while a cup of drip has more in total. B is more complete, adding the double shot (about 125 mg), larger mugs and a note that amounts vary. The 200 mg figure for a 12-ounce mug is at the high end but plausible. A is correct but thinner and lists sources it never cites.

Both answers are correct: espresso has more caffeine per ounce, but a normal cup of drip has more in total. A also covers double shots and says amounts vary by bean, roast and brewing, which is useful practical context. B is accurate but repeats itself, skips the double shot and lists two sources it never uses. A is clearer and more complete.

B explains accurately what each one is (a cell versus genetic material in a protein coat), why antibiotics have no target in a virus, what treats viral infections instead, and the risk of antibiotic resistance. Its sources are reputable. A is thin and states that viruses aren't alive as settled fact. It cites only one of its four sources, and that one is a study guide.

A is accurate and fully answers both parts: how the two differ in structure and replication, and why antibiotics have no target in a virus. It also covers antivirals and the resistance risk, all well sourced. B is correct but thin. It flatly says viruses are "not alive", which is actually debated, and it cites only one of the four sources it lists.

A makes serious false claims: that Windows has no user/group ownership and no execute permission. It never mentions NTFS ACLs, and its points about Samba and permission transfer are muddled. B accurately covers Linux owner/group/other bits, special bits, NTFS ACLs, inheritance, null vs. empty DACL, and POSIX ACLs, and stays grounded in its sources.

Answer A accurately explains both models: Linux owner/group/others rwx, special bits and POSIX ACLs, and Windows NTFS ACLs with ordered allow/deny entries, inheritance and auditing. Answer B wrongly says Windows has no file ownership and no fine-grained permissions, and it never mentions ACLs. Its claims about execution and Samba are also muddled or wrong.

B is better. It covers Luther's aim to reform the Church from within, the Ninety-five Theses, faith alone, his excommunication and outlawing, the lasting split in Western Christianity and his German Bible, with accurate dates. A is correct but thin: it never says the Church split, and its cited source [3] goes unused.

A is accurate: reform from within, the 1517 Theses, faith alone, excommunication in 1521, Worms, the lasting Catholic–Protestant split and the 1534 Bible. B is accurate but thin. It omits the split, oversimplifies Bible interpretation and lists source [3] without citing it. A covers both parts more fully.

A's main claim is circular: it says AI is the technology behind AI's foundation. It gets Dartmouth 1956 right, and several of its listed sources look unrelated. B correctly names the programmable digital computer and Dartmouth's 1956 workshop. Its accurate details (organizers, McCarthy coining the term, Logic Theorist) fit its sources. B is clearly better.

A correctly names the programmable digital computer and Dartmouth (1956), with accurate details that its sources support. B circularly says AI's foundational technology is AI, which fails the main part of the question. It gets Dartmouth and the Logic Theorist right but lists sources it never uses.

Both answers correctly name the Danube and the Black Sea, so both fully answer the question. B adds accurate extras: Buda and Pest, about 28 km through the city, about 2,850 km long, ten countries, and the delta. These details are sourced but don't change the answer, and A is more concise. Neither is clearly better.

Both answers correctly say the Danube flows through Budapest and empties into the Black Sea. A's extra details are accurate: Buda and Pest, the Black Forest source, about 2,850 km, ten countries and the delta. They aren't needed, though. B answers both parts concisely, which suits a phone. Neither is clearly better.

Answer A says Peru's language is Quechua and leaves out Spanish, the dominant language, so its answer is misleading. Its sources are about the Inca Empire, not modern Peru. Answer B correctly names Spanish as the main language and lists all three official languages (Spanish, Quechua, Aymara). Its census figures (about 83% and 13%) are accurate and match its sources.

A correctly names Cusco and Peru, gives Spanish as the main language, and lists Quechua and Aymara as co-official, with census figures that hold up. B wrongly gives Quechua as Peru's language and leaves out Spanish, which most Peruvians speak. B's sources cover the Inca Empire, not modern Peru, so they don't back its claim.

Answer A is wrong and contradicts itself. It names Edward VII but gives his reign as 1901–1910, which began after the tower was finished in 1889. Answer B correctly names Queen Victoria, who reigned 1837–1901. Its supporting details are accurate: the tower was finished on 31 March 1889, about 52 years into her reign and two years after her 1887 Golden Jubilee.

A is right: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, which covers the tower's completion on 31 March 1889. Its other details are accurate and supported by its sources. B names Edward VII, which is wrong. B's own dates show his reign began in 1901, after the tower was finished, so the answer contradicts itself.

A is wrong: Berners-Lee studied at Oxford (Queen's College), not Southampton. A treats his later academic post as where he studied, misreading its own source, and pastes in raw source text. B gives the right university, college, years and degree, and adds well-supported details such as the homemade computer and the hacking ban.

A correctly names Oxford (Queen's College, first-class physics degree, 1973–76), and its extra details are accurate. B wrongly says Southampton: its source lists him as an academic who worked there, not a student. B's text is also garbled and repetitive, with stray citations.

Both answers correctly identify Japan and Mount Fuji at 3,776 m. A undercuts itself by naming Fuji and then concluding the answer "cannot be determined," which is confusing and unhelpful, though it is honest about what its sources lack. B answers directly with accurate, sourced details, so B is better.

A correctly identifies Tokyo/Japan and Mount Fuji (3,776 m), with accurate supporting details and relevant sources. B mentions Fuji's height but then contradicts itself by concluding the answer "cannot be determined." That is confusing and unhelpful, even though B is honest about what its sources contain. A is clearly better.

Both answers correctly say the currency is the Cambodian riel. A cites Angkor Wat pages for the currency and then admits those sources don't mention it, so its citations contradict themselves. B cites currency sources and adds accurate, practical context: US dollars are widely used, riel comes as small change, and the government is promoting the riel. B is better grounded and more useful.

A correctly names the riel and notes that US dollars are widely used, especially in Siem Reap, with fitting sources. B also gets the riel right but leaves out the dollar. It cites Angkor Wat pages for the currency, then admits they don't mention it. That contradicts itself and weakens its grounding. A is clearer and more useful.

Answer A is accurate but generic. It ties no specific claim to its sources and leaves out the mechanisms. Answer B gives concrete details that match standard accounts and the cited sources: the Theses spreading within weeks, Luther's huge print output, cheap pamphlets read aloud, the vernacular Bible, and the Rubin-style city evidence. It also notes the scholarly debate fairly.

A gives a specific, accurate account: the Theses spreading fast, Luther's output, cheap vernacular pamphlets read aloud, the vernacular Bible, and the city-level evidence along with the scholarly debate over it. Its figures are plausible and tied to sources. B is correct but generic, with no specifics or mechanisms, and its citations add little. A is clearly better.

A states a poorly supported floor-vibration story as fact, implies he was fully deaf throughout, names only the Ninth, and cites an irrelevant forum thread. B is accurate: hearing loss from about 1798, the 1802 Heiligenstadt Testament, inner hearing, sketchbooks, conversation books. It hedges the folklore and lists the major works.

A is accurate: hearing loss from about 1798, the 1802 Heiligenstadt Testament, conversation books, and middle and late works including the 1824 Ninth. It flags the rod-biting story as unverified. B states the doubtful floor-lying claim as fact, names only the Ninth, and cites a sci-fi forum. B is thin and weakly grounded.

A's 26.5 matches total France by chance, but its France area (68,605,616 m², 0.0686M km²) is wrong and 17,098,242÷0.0686 isn't 26.5. No France source is cited. B's figures and ratios (≈31 for European France, ≈26–27 including overseas regions) are correct and sourced, and it explains which definition gives which answer.

A's numbers are right: 17.1M/551,695 ≈ 31 for mainland France and 17.1M/643,801 ≈ 26.6 including overseas regions. It covers both readings clearly. B gives France 68,605,616 m² (about 69 km², likely the population figure), and its working (17.1M ÷ 0.0686 ≠ 26.5) is wrong. Its answer is right only by accident, and France's area isn't supported by its Russia-only sources.

A wrongly says Germany is denser, treating total population as density, and cites an irrelevant source. B is correct: about 541 vs. 240 per km², so about 2.25 times as dense by land area, or about 1.8 times including water. Its arithmetic checks out, its figures are sourced and it is concise.

A gives the right answer, about 2× as dense, and handles the land-versus-total-area question correctly. Its Germany figure of about 240/km² is slightly high; Destatis reports about 233. B wrongly answers "no" because it confuses total population with density, and it contradicts its own 541/km² figure. B also cites an irrelevant source.

Both answers correctly give about 1.3 million Earths by volume. B also explains the math (109³ ≈ 1.3 million) and adds a valid packing caveat: equal spheres fill at most about 74% of a space, so roughly 960,000 whole Earths would fit. Its sources back these points. A is correct but bare. B is more complete and more useful while staying concise.

Both correctly give about 1.3 million by volume. A also explains why: 109³ is about 1.3 million. It adds the real-world limit that tightly packed whole spheres fill only about 74% of the space, giving roughly 960,000. Its sources plausibly support this. B is correct and grounded but bare, with no explanation or caveat. A is more complete and informative.

A ignores the given 5 km/h, uses 0.9 m/s and miscomputes even that (should be ~6,542 h, not 7,385). It takes the wall's length from an unrelated source and adds irrelevant Badaling filler. B uses the correct 21,196 km figure with sound math (~4,240 h, 177 days), adds the Ming-wall case and realistic caveats, and is well sourced.

A uses the 5 km/h speed the question gives, and its maths is correct: 21,196 km takes about 4,240 hours, or 177 days nonstop. It also covers the Ming-wall figure, a realistic daily walking pace and the caveat about terrain. B swaps in 0.9 m/s instead of 5 km/h, and its figure is still wrong (it should be about 6,540 hours). It also pads with irrelevant Badaling travel details.

Both subtract correctly (4,043.27 m from the 2023 Mont Blanc figure). A gives a precise figure as if fixed, ignores that Mont Blanc's ice cap changes height between surveys, and cites vague sources. B dates both measurements, admits it found no official 2025 result, and rounds sensibly to about 4,040 m. B is more grounded and robust.

Both get 8,848.86 − 4,805.59 = 4,043.27 m right. A adds that Mont Blanc's ice-cap summit changes height and says it couldn't confirm the 2025 survey, so it gives a sensible ~4,040 m answer. B gives 4,043.27 as exact and current, with no caveat and vague sources. A is better.

B is accurate and grounded. It cites the CDC, explains that the water gets contaminated in the pipes and storage tanks after leaving treatment, and gives practical advice on garrafones and ice. A overstates the contamination and garbles the 87% statistic so it reads as contradictory. It also lists an irrelevant source about Morocco, and its ice advice is overly broad.

A is accurate and well grounded: it cites CDC advice, explains that contamination happens in the distribution system (old pipes, sinking ground, rooftop tanks) and mentions local jug use. B overstates the contamination and garbles the 87% statistic. Its claim that ice is often not purified is doubtful, and it cites an irrelevant source about Morocco.

Both give the right answer: no tipping. A says "many restaurants" add a 10% service charge, which overstates it, since that's mostly upscale or hotel restaurants. B is accurate and more complete. It covers service charges at upscale places, otoshi and seating fees, and how to thank staff instead, all backed by its cited sources.

Both are right that you don't tip in Japan. A is accurate and complete: it notes that service charges appear mainly at upscale places, explains otoshi and seating charges, and suggests saying thanks instead. B is correct but thin, and saying "many restaurants" add a 10% charge overstates it, since this is mostly upscale venues and hotels.

B gives current, cited guidance: rinse with seawater, use hot-water immersion for pain, avoid urine and other myths, treat vinegar use as species-dependent, and know when to call emergency services. A leaves out hot-water treatment and pain relief, gives an outdated shaving-cream step, and treats vinegar as the default for most stings. It also cites only one of its claims.

A gives accurate, current advice: rinse with seawater, lift tentacles off safely, use hot water for pain, use vinegar only depending on species, and call for help at red-flag signs. B tells people to use vinegar by default and suggests shaving cream, both outdated. It also leaves out pain relief and leans on weak home-remedy sources with sparse citations.

Both give the correct Thai words. A mentions a polite marker but never names it, wrongly says it ends every phrase, and cites sources that don't apply. B explains ครับ/ค่ะ by gender, gives full example phrases and notes that ขอโทษ also means "sorry". B has one small mistake: it calls the vowel in "khop" short when it is actually long. B is clearly better.

A gets both phrases right, names the male and female polite endings, and notes that ขอโทษ also means "sorry." Its only slip is calling the vowel in "khop" short. B gets the words right but never names the endings and implies they are part of the words. It also cites irrelevant sources (a Japanese phrasebook, English Q&A).

B is accurate and closely follows CDC guidance. It covers mild symptoms, the danger signs of HACE and HAPE, Peru-specific altitudes, ascent rules, Diamox and when to descend. A gives thin symptom coverage, uses a scouting source, leaves out warning signs and descent, and adds irrelevant advice about getting lost off-trail.

A is accurate and complete. It covers mild altitude sickness, the dangerous brain and lung forms, Cusco and Inca Trail heights, safe ascent pacing, avoiding alcohol and Diamox. B is thin and misses the danger signs, descending and medication. It leans on coca tea and adds unrelated advice about getting lost off-trail. Citing a Scouting merit badge page for symptoms is weak.

A gets the September–March window right, but it blames poor summer viewing on "light pollution" when the real cause is bright summer nights. Its sources are also thin, and it gives no tips. B is accurate and gives more: the equinox peaks, the 9 pm–2 am window, and why cloud cover matters, with practical tips. B is better.

A is accurate and practical: it gives the season, why the equinox months are good, viewing hours, and tips about clouds and forecasts. B gets two things wrong. It says winter nights are "shorter" when they are longer, and it blames "light pollution" when the real cause is summer daylight. B is also thin and gives no practical advice.

B is better. It gives a concrete plan grouped by area, with the key sights (Fushimi Inari, Kiyomizu-dera, Kinkaku-ji, Arashiyama, Gion) and accurate tips for avoiding crowds. A stays close to its sources but is vague. It leaves out almost every major sight and calls the self-guided pamphlet a "guided tour," so it's of little practical use.

A gives a concrete, accurate two-day plan grouped by area, naming the key sights: Arashiyama, Kinkaku-ji, Fushimi Inari, Kiyomizu-dera and Gion. Its crowd-timing tips are correct, and Fushimi Inari is open 24 hours. B is vague, names few landmarks and leans on a possibly outdated pamphlet. Its plan is thin and hard to act on.

B is accurate and specific: it covers Kenya's yellow fever entry rule, the CDC's regional exceptions, hepatitis B for unvaccinated travelers under 60, and malaria below 2,500 m. It also says it couldn't check the Ministry of Health page. A treats hepatitis A/B and meningitis as routine, garbles the immune globulin advice, omits the entry rule and repeats one source three times.

A is accurate: it covers the yellow fever entry rule and the areas where the shot isn't recommended, routine and travel vaccines, and malaria, and it admits its limits. B wrongly calls hepatitis A/B and meningitis routine and garbles the immune globulin advice. B also omits Kenya's yellow fever entry requirement and repeats sources.

B is far more complete and useful. It gives accurate legal context (Scotland, Dartmoor 2025, England/Wales) and correct Leave No Trace details. However, it falsely claims to live in Scotland. It also calls the two-to-three-night limit "unwritten" when the Access Code states it. A is sourced but thin: it relies on stealth-camping tips and skips water, waste and fire guidance.

A is accurate on legality (Scottish access code, England/Wales trespass, the 2025 Dartmoor ruling) and on Leave No Trace practice. It falsely claims to live in Scotland, though, and the two-to-three-night rule is written in the Scottish code, not unwritten. B is thin and leans on stealth-camping advice like using restaurants. It skips waste disposal and water treatment.

B is accurate and covers both parts: good foods, kitchen scraps and harmful foods, each with a reason. It notes that the toxic list comes from pet-bird sources. A is thin, says almost nothing on what to avoid, and adds off-topic advice about coyotes and deer that misreads its source.

A covers both parts accurately: safe foods, plus a solid avoid-list with reasons. It is open that the toxic list comes mostly from pet-bird guidance. B is thin and barely addresses what not to feed. It adds an irrelevant point about coyotes and deer and misses key hazards such as bread, salt, avocado and chocolate.

A has you take the whole hinge off without needing to, never says to lubricate the pin, and contradicts itself on lithium grease vs. WD-40. Its mortise advice is off-topic. B gives a quick fix, then a safe step-by-step fix: one hinge at a time, clean the pin, lubricate it, then tighten or replace the hinge. It is accurate, sourced and easy to follow.

A gives clear, accurate steps: a quick spray fix, then the full method of pulling, cleaning and greasing the pin, plus fallbacks. B overcomplicates things by unscrewing the hinges, never says to grease the pin, and contradicts itself: grease "lasts longer but may need more frequent application." B's mortise advice comes from an unrelated thread about a door touching its frame.

A is thin. It stops at day 3 and never covers discarding, ongoing feeding or how to tell the starter is ready. Its yeast aside is off-topic. B gives the full process: amounts, daily then twice-daily feeds, temperature, the common day 3–4 slump and clear signs of readiness. Its claims are accurate and attributed to sources. B is clearly better.

A gives a complete, accurate timeline with feeding ratios, temperature, troubleshooting (the day 3 lull and hooch) and signs that the starter is ready, all tied to sources. B stops at day 3 with no feeding, discard or readiness guidance. It also adds off-topic alternatives, including a confusing note about commercial yeast. A is clearly better.

B gives correct ss syntax with clear flag explanations, plus lsof and fuser, why sudo is needed, and container/namespace tips. A's lsof command is right, but it wrongly says netstat -tnp lists listening ports (that needs -l), and it gives no ss syntax.
